Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies, extending to them affection, while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and yourselves [from your homeland] because you believe in Allah, your Lord. If you have gone out for jihad in My cause and seeking My approval...﴾.

The exegetes agreed, and it is established in the sound narrations, that this verse was revealed concerning the matter of the letter that Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, an ally of Banu Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza from Quraysh, wrote. Hatib was one of the Muhajirun, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and one of the people of Badr.

The summary of the story, drawn from the sound reports and the well-known biography, is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had prepared to set out intending Makkah. It was said that this was for the sake of 'Umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and this is the most correct view; and it was said that it was for the conquest of Makkah, but this does not hold. At that time a woman named Sarah, a freedwoman of Abu 'Amr ibn Sayfi ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf, came from Makkah to Madinah, and she was upon the religion of polytheism. She said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "You were the family, the clients, the origin and the tribe, and the clients have gone (meaning those of her clients who were killed on the Day of Badr). Need has pressed upon me, so I have come to you that you may give me and clothe me." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib and the Banu al-Muttalib to give her, so they clothed her, gave her, and provided her with a mount. Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah came to her and gave her a letter to deliver to those in Makkah to whom he had written, informing them of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ resolve to set out against them, and he hired her for delivering it. So she set out. Allah revealed this to His Messenger ﷺ, and he sent 'Ali, al-Zubayr, al-Miqdad and Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, and they were horsemen. He said: "Set out until you reach Rawdat Khakh, for there is a woman there carrying a letter from Hatib to the polytheists. Take it from her and let her go her way." So they set out, their horses racing with them, until they reached Rawdat Khakh, and there they found the woman.

[Page 133]

They said: "Bring out the letter." She said: "I have no letter." They said: "You will bring out the letter, or we will strip you of your clothes" (meaning that they would strip her naked). So she brought it out from her braids; in another narration, from her waistband.

They brought it to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "O Hatib, what is this?" He said: "Do not hasten against me, O Messenger of Allah. I was a man attached to Quraysh, and those of the Muhajirun who were with you had relatives who protect their families by them, so I loved, since I had lost that lineage among them, to make among them a hand that would protect my relatives" — he meant his mother and his brothers — "and I did not do it out of disbelief, nor apostasy from my religion, nor contentment with disbelief after Islam." The Prophet ﷺ said: "He has spoken the truth." 'Umar said: "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite, O Messenger of Allah." The Prophet ﷺ said: "He has witnessed Badr, and what will make you know? Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you." And he said: "Do not say to Hatib anything but good." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies...﴾ the verses.

It is apparent that the woman came as a spy, for it is reported in some narrations that the Prophet ﷺ did not grant safety on the Day of Conquest to four people, and this woman was among them. But this is contradicted by what comes in the narration of the story, in the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Take the letter from her and let her go her way."

The prohibition has been addressed to all the believers, as a warning against doing what Hatib did.

Al-'Aduww (the enemy) is one who has enmity; it is a fa'ul in the sense of fa'il, from 'ada ya'du, like 'afuw. Its origin is a verbal noun, on the pattern of fa'ul, like qabul and similar from the few verbal nouns of this pattern. But since it is in the pattern of verbal nouns, it is treated as a verbal noun, so that in describing with it the masculine and the feminine, the singular, the dual and the plural are alike. Allah the Exalted said ﴿For they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and it was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿If he was from a people hostile to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 92] in Surat al-Nisa.

The meaning: do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies. What is meant is enmity in religion, for the believers did not begin hostility toward them; rather, the polytheists displayed hostility toward the believers in defense of their polytheism, so they counted those who had left polytheism as their enemies. The polytheists of the Arabs varied in their hostility toward the Muslims; for Khuza'ah were polytheists yet were allies of the Prophet ﷺ.

[Page 134]

So the meaning of the attribution of "enemy" to the first person pronoun ya' is on the estimate: enemy of My religion, or of My Messenger.

Al-ittikhadh (taking) is an ifti'al from al-akhdh (taking). The iftiʿāl form is used for intensifying the taking in a figurative sense, so it is applied to being engaged with and constant attachment. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿O you who have believed, take your precaution﴾ [al-Nisa: 71] in Surat al-Nisa. For this reason, after its object there necessarily follows a state (ḥāl) to specify the aspect of dealing, whether good or bad. So this verb is treated like ṣayyara (to make into). The state following it is considered in the position of a second object, because its mention is necessary; and whether the second object of the verbs of ẓanna and its sisters is anything but a ḥāl in meaning has been discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am: 74] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿you extend to them affection﴾ is in the position of a state from the pronoun in (do not take), or in the position of a description of (allies), or an explanation of the meaning of taking them as allies.

It is also permissible that it be a clause in the position of a state from the pronoun in (do not take), because making it a state leads to expressing astonishment at their extending affection to them.

The basic meaning of al-ilqa' is throwing what is in the hand onto the ground. It is used figuratively for casting something without reflection on its place, that is, you direct your affection toward them without deliberation. Allah the Exalted said ﴿So they cast to them the word, "You are indeed liars"﴾ [al-Nahl: 86], discussed in Surat al-Nahl.

The bi in (bil-mawaddah) serves to emphasize the connection of the verb with its object. The original phrasing is: you cast to them affection, like His saying ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195] and His saying ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. This is a depiction of the strength of their affection for them.

The depiction of this state is intensified by the clause of state that follows it, which is ﴿while they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾, and it is a state from the pronoun in (to them) or from (My enemy).

﴿What has come to you of the truth﴾ is the Qur'an and the religion. It is mentioned by way of a relative construction so that it encompasses everything the Messenger ﷺ brought them, in a concise manner, together with what the relative clause implies of condemning their disbelief, that it is disbelief in what the seekers of guidance should not disbelieve in, for the truth is beloved and desired.

[Page 135]

The transitive use of jaa' (came) to the pronoun of the addressees, who are those who have believed, is because they are the ones who benefited from that truth and accepted it, so it is as if it came to them and not to others; otherwise it came to call both those who believed and the polytheists, and those who believed accepted it while the polytheists rejected it.

In this there is an allusion that the disbelief of the disbelievers in it arises from their envy of those who believed before them.

In that there is also a stirring of the hearts of the believers, so that they may beware of allying with the polytheists.

The clause ﴿they expel the Messenger and yourselves﴾ is a state from the pronoun in (disbelieved), meaning: they did not content themselves with their disbelief in what came of the truth, but joined with it the expulsion of the Messenger ﷺ and your expulsion from your land, because you believe in Allah your Lord. That is, this is aggression which they were driven to because you believed in Allah your Lord; and there is no excuse for them in it, because your faith does not harm them. For this reason the Name of Majesty was followed by the description "your Lord," in the manner of His saying ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship... To you your religion, and to me my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1-6].

This state is related in the present tense to depict the situation, because the clause, when it occurred as a state from the pronoun in (and they have disbelieved), the expulsion of the Messenger ﷺ and the believers in that condition was a monstrous act, so it is intended to evoke the image of that great expulsion, to convey the monstrousness of their pursuing it.

The expulsion is meant as: inciting them to leave by bringing about the causes of departure, through constriction upon the Muslims and harm to them.

The expulsion is attributed to the whole pronoun of the enemy, because all of them were content with what some of them did of harming the Muslims. Perhaps they incited their foolish ones against them; for this reason the expulsion is figurative in its causes, while its attribution to the polytheists is literal.

These attributes together apply only to the polytheists of Makkah, and their combined presence is the reason for the prohibition against befriending them.

The present tense was used in His saying (that you believe) to indicate the continuity of the believers' faith, and in it there is an allusion to praising the believers for their steadfastness in their religion, and that what caused them to leave their lands did not turn them away from it.

[Page 136]

His saying ﴿If you have gone out for jihad in My cause and seeking My approval﴾ is a conditional clause, appended to the prohibition in His saying ﴿do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾. This is a context in which the conditional is used as a completion (tatmim) for what precedes it, without intending to make what precedes contingent upon the content of the protasis, that is, it is not intended that if the protasis fails, what was conditioned upon it fails, as is the usual case with conditionals. Rather, the intent is to affirm the preceding speech with the content of the protasis, so it functions like a causal explanation for what precedes. It is expressed in the form of a condition only because the speaker is confident that the content of the protasis is realized, such that the listener would not expect that the content of the protasis fails to occur; so the conditional form is meant as a warning, by way of the figurative sense of the compound, because the meaning of a condition ordinarily implies doubt. For this reason such a conditional is used when the speaker is certain that its content is realized and is certain of the truth of what he says before the condition. As mentioned in the Kashshaf at His saying ﴿We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 51], in the reading of the one who read (in kuntu awwala al-mu'minin) with a kasra on the hamza of (in), which is an anomalous reading, making (in) conditional, even though they were certain that they were the first of the believers; so they hoped for the forgiveness of their sins because of their certainty that they were the first of the believers. Thus the conditional in such a case functions like a causal explanation, and the conditional particle is like idh or the lam of causation.

Someone may also use such a conditional to make clear the obligation to act according to what the content of the protasis requires, and not to contradict its requirement, as in His saying ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] up to His saying ﴿if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], that is: your faith and certainty in what We sent down require that you accept the disposal of the spoils to the specified categories by Allah's command.

There is much of this in the Qur'an, if you survey its occurrences.

In such a conditional it is common for the protasis to be a verb of being (kana), as a notice that the condition is certainly realized.

What occurs in this surah of this kind is intended to affirm the prohibition against taking the enemy of Allah as allies, and it is followed by a conditional whose condition is trusted to be fulfilled, since those who were prohibited are undoubtedly engaged in the content of the protasis; so mentioning the condition adds emphasis to the restraint.

For this reason such a conditional is placed at the end of a speech, since it resembles completion (tatmim) and conclusion (tadhyil), and this is one of the subtleties of usage in eloquent speech.

[Page 137]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, on His words, ﴿Had he not persevered in devotion to our gods, he would almost have led us astray from them﴾ [al-Furqan: 42], in Surah al-Furqan: "Law (lawla) in this kind of speech operates, in meaning and not in its grammatical construction, as a restriction on an unrestricted ruling." He also said here, ﴿if you have indeed gone out﴾ is related to ﴿do not take﴾. The statement of the grammarians about such a construction, that it is a conditional clause whose apodosis (jawab, the answer of the condition) is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, is different. He means that there is a difference between the grammarians' statement and what he chose, namely making it related to ﴿do not take﴾, since he made the apodosis of the condition not implied. I say: his statement should be counted among the distinctions in the use of conditionals, like the distinctions in the predicate and the distinctions of the circumstantial clause (hal), which both are chapter-headed in the book Dala'il al-I'jaz (Proofs of Inimitability). The statement of the grammarians follows the general state of conditionals that come after their answer, such as: "Accept the intercession of so-and-so if he intercedes with you." It is appropriate to seek, for the placing before of what indicates the omitted answer when it is omitted, a subtle purpose outside the usual use of the conditional, serving as a completion and a finishing touch.

The conditional particle in such a construction resembles the concessive "in" (in, "even if") and the concessive "law" (law, "even if"). For this reason al-Zamakhshari said here that the clause ﴿if you have indeed gone out﴾ is related to ﴿do not take﴾, meaning the relation of a circumstantial clause to its governing verb, i.e., "while the state is that you went out in the way of God and sought His good pleasure," on the basis that the condition of the concessive "in" and "law" is regarded as a circumstance (hal). That the condition of these two is accompanied by the particle of circumstance (waw al-hal) does not object to this, because Ibn Jinni and al-Zamakhshari permitted the circumstantial clause in such a construction to be free of the waw, and usage supports them.

The meaning: there must not occur from you the taking of My enemy and your enemy as allies and the cultivation of their affection, while they have disbelieved in what came to you of the truth, and have expelled you because of your faith. ﴿If you have indeed gone out from your lands striving in My cause and seeking My good pleasure﴾, how then can you befriend those who expelled you, when their expelling you was for My sake, and I am your Lord?

What is meant by "going out" in His words ﴿if you have indeed gone out﴾ is going out from Makkah as emigrants (muhajarah) to Madinah. The address is therefore specific to the emigrants, in the manner of the specification of a general term (takhsis al-'umum), in His words ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾. In this specification, the context of the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was taken into account, namely the incident of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah.

﴿Striving (jihadan)﴾ and ﴿seeking My good pleasure (ibtigha'a mardatee)﴾ are two verbal nouns in the accusative as objects of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, the object indicating the reason for the action).

* * *

[Page 138]

﴿You reveal to them affection, while I know best what you conceal and what you disclose﴾.

It is permissible for this clause to be an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿you send them affection﴾, or a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, where the second term is included in the first) from it, since revealing to them in secret the affection is among what is included in sending affection to them. The statement is used for reproach and wonder: the reproach is derived from placing the statement immediately after the prior prohibition, and the wonder is derived from its being followed by the clause ﴿while I know best what you conceal and what you disclose﴾, meaning: how do you think that your secret dealings with them are hidden from us, and that We do not inform Our Messenger about them?

Al-Israr (revealing in secret) means speaking and informing in secret.

The object of ﴿you reveal﴾ may be omitted, indicated by the context, meaning: you inform them in secret of the condition of the Muslims.

The present tense form is used to depict the state of secretly revealing to them, to make it appear more abominable.

The ba' in ﴿with affection (bil-mawaddah)﴾ indicates causation, meaning: you inform them secretly because of affection, i.e., because of seeking their affection for you, as is the case in the matter of Hatib's letter.

It is permissible that ﴿with affection﴾ occupies the position of the object of the verb ﴿you reveal﴾, with the ba' being superfluous, to emphasize the objective relation, like the ba' in His words ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

The clause ﴿while I know best what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿you reveal﴾, or parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the waw is the parenthetical waw.

This is the locus of the wonder at the act of the one alluded to, who is Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah. The placing first of concealing is because it is the appropriate match for His words ﴿I know best﴾, and because it agrees with the story.

"A'lamu" (I know best) is an elative noun (ism al-tafdil, a comparative/superlative form), and the thing compared is known from His words ﴿you reveal to them﴾. The estimated meaning is: "I know best, of them and of you, what you conceal and what you disclose."

The ba' is connected to the elative noun and is in the sense of accompaniment.

* * *

﴿And whoever does that among you has certainly strayed from the right way﴾.

[Page 139]

It is conjoined to the prohibitive clause in His words ﴿do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾. Conjoined to the prohibition is a warning that whoever does not desist from what he was forbidden has strayed from guidance.

The pronoun of absence in ﴿does that (yaf'aluhu)﴾ refers to the taking, understood from the verb of ﴿do not take My enemy﴾, meaning: whoever does that after this prohibition and warning, he has strayed from the right way.

﴿The right way (sawa' al-sabil)﴾ is used metaphorically for righteous deeds and guidance, because of their resemblance to the level road that brings whoever travels it to his goal, while whoever deviates from it falls into ruin. What is meant here is that he has strayed from Islam and strayed from right conduct.

The word ﴿whoever (man)﴾ is conditional, and the verb after it is in the future, and it is a threat to those who do what Hatib did after the prohibition, the warning, the reproach, and the making abominable of his act had reached them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 2:

﴿If they overcome you, they will be your enemies and will stretch out their hands and their tongues against you with evil, and they wish that you would disbelieve.﴾ This sentence conveys the sense of giving a reason for the implication of His words, ﴿Then he has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], with regard to part of what this sentence conveys, which is straying from right guidance. For it may be hidden, and one may suppose that there is benefit in seeking the affection of the enemy, as is the case with the hypocrites described in His words, ﴿Those who wait and watch you: if there is a victory for you from Allah, they say, "Were we not with you?" but if the disbelievers have a share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?"﴾ [al-Nisa': 141]. Thus one may suppose that their friendship is a form of shrewdness and prudence, hoping to benefit from them if the state turns in their favour. So Allah made clear to them the error of this supposition, and that if they benefit from their affection by gaining knowledge of their strength, and then prepare against them and prevail over them, they will not observe with regard to them any kinship or covenant. And that if they seize them and gain power over them, they will be enemies to them, because one who has harboured enmity for a long time finds it hard to turn into a loving friend, owing to the intensity of the rage at what they have suffered from the Muslims, namely the nullification of the religion of polytheism and the belittling of its people and their idols.

The verb (yakununu) indicates that their enmity is ancient and that it will continue.

And "al-basṭ" (stretching out) is used metaphorically for increase, because it is commonly understood that abundance is likened to breadth and length, and its opposite, restraint (al-qabḍ), is likened to the opposite of that. So "basṭ al-yad" means increasing its activity.

What is meant here is the activity of the hand that causes harm, such as striking, shackling and stabbing, and the activity of the tongue that causes injury, such as insult and mockery. This is indicated by His words "with evil," which is connected to (yabsuṭū), whose object is ﴿their hands and their tongues﴾.

The clause ﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in (yakununu), and the waw is the waw of circumstance, meaning: they already now wish that you would disbelieve; so how much more so if they capture you? Is not the most important thing to them at that time that they should return you as disbelievers? Thus the circumstantial clause serves as evidence for an implied conjunct to the answer of the condition, as if it were said: "If they overcome you, they will be your enemies, and so on, and will return you as disbelievers." The clause ﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ is not coordinated with the clause of the answer, because their desire that the Muslims disbelieve is a desire not restricted by the condition. For this reason the verb (waddū) came in the past tense and not in the present like the three verbs before it, (yathqafūkum), (yakūnū lakum aʿdāʾan), and (yabsuṭū), so that it would be known that it is not coordinated with the answer of the condition.

This interpretation is better than what is found in al-Qazwini's book al-Iḍāḥ, in the discussion of restricting the predicate by a condition, where he inclined to hold that ﴿and they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿if they overcome you﴾.

He compared it with the clause ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 111] in His words, ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 111]. For the clause introduced by (thumma) there is a conjunct to the whole of the condition with its verb and its answer, not to the clause of the condition's verb alone.

And (law) here is verbal-masdarian (maṣdariyyah), so the verb (takfurūn) is interpreted as a verbal noun, meaning: they wish your disbelief.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 60, verse 3:**

﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection. He will separate between you. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

He moved from explaining the evil outcome of allying with the enemies of the religion in this worldly life to explaining the evil outcome of that alliance in the Hereafter. The good transition is supported by His saying ﴿and they wish you would disbelieve﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2], which indicates that their desire for your disbelief, before they gain power over you, turns into their compelling you to disbelieve once they do gain power over you. Therefore your close relatives, such as your mothers, your full brothers and your maternal relatives, will not benefit you, nor will your children, and they will not shield you from the punishment of the Hereafter, even if they benefited you in this world through maintaining ties of kinship and supporting your children.

The sentence ﴿Your relatives and your children will not benefit you…﴾ to its end is a resumptive sentence (istinaf bayani), arising from an assumed question by the one who hears the sentence ﴿and they wish you would disbelieve﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2]. That is, it is fitting that one asks about its consequences, given how serious the matter is.

If it arose from a statement that served as a reason (ta'lil) for the sentence ﴿then he has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], then it also gives a second reason in meaning. Were it not for the intention of the explanatory resumption, this sentence would have come conjoined with the waw to the one before it. What made this more fitting is that what came from Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, and what was counted against him, is an alliance with the enemy. He excused himself by saying that he wanted to gain a hand among the polytheists by which they would protect his relatives (namely his mother and brothers). For this reason, the negation of benefit began with mention of relatives, to match the story of Hatib, since the mother is a relative and her sons are his brothers, his kin.

As for the conjunction of ﴿nor your children﴾, it is a completion (tatmim) to make the prohibition include people who had children in Makkah.

By "relatives" is meant those who are related by kinship (dhawu al-arham), with an omitted modifier, because the context makes it clear.

﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an adverbial of time that can be governed by both the verb ﴿will not benefit you﴾ and the verb ﴿He will separate between you﴾. This is because it is not required that both governing verbs precede the governed element when it is an adverb of time, since adverbs of time may precede their governing verbs. If you reject this dispute (tanazu'), then say it is the adverb of ﴿will not benefit you﴾, and take the verb ﴿He will separate between you﴾ as having an omitted adverb, indicated by what is mentioned.

Here, "fasl" means separation, not judgment. The meaning is: on the Day of Resurrection, you and your relatives and children will be separated, with one group in Paradise and another in the Blaze. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother, his mother and his father, his wife and his children. For every man among them that Day will be a matter that occupies him﴾ [Abasa: 34–37].

[Page 142]

The meaning is that they will not benefit you on the Day of Resurrection, so why do you abandon the right of Allah out of consideration for them, when they will flee from you on the Day when the terror intensifies? This corrects their opinion about allying with the disbelievers, first by what pertains to the condition of those they allied with, and then, secondly, by what pertains to the condition of those for whose sake they engaged in the alliance. This is a comprehensive division, indicating that whatever Hatib undertook is an error and falsehood from any perspective from which it is viewed.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿yufsalu baynakum﴾ with the verb ﴿yufsalu﴾ in the passive voice and lightened (mukhaffafan). 'Asim and Ya'qub read ﴿yafsilu﴾ in the active voice, with its subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, known from the context. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿yufassilu﴾ with the sad doubled and vowelled with kasra, in the active voice, for emphasis in separation (mubalaghah fi al-fasl), with the subject being a pronoun referring to Allah, known from the context.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿yufassalu﴾ with a damma on the yā' and a doubled and fathah-vowelled sad, in the passive voice of the doubled form of faṣṣala, with a deputy subject (nā'ib al-fa'il).

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ contains both a warning and a promise.

[Page 143]

The opening of this verse serves to emphasise the content of the clause ﴿if they overpower you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2] and the clause ﴿your relatives will not benefit you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 3]. This is because, by what it contains, namely that those addressed by the rebuke opposed the excellent example, it strengthens the affirmation of the error that merits the rebuke.

This is because, after finishing the explanation of the error of one who allies with the enemy of Allah, with what that brings upon its people of harms in this world and in the Hereafter as a warning to them against it, the discourse moved on to presenting the righteous conduct through an example from the actions of the people of sincere faith and upright steadfastness. And how excellent an example it is.

The opening of the speech with the two words ﴿qad kānat﴾ (there has indeed been) is for emphasising the report. For ﴿qad﴾ together with the verb of being is used to imply a reproach, a rebuke of the addressee for turning away from acting upon what the report contains. Like the saying of ʿUmar to Ibn ʿAbbas on the day the slave of al-Mughirah stabbed him: "You and your father used to love that these non-Arabs would multiply in Medina." And from it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering﴾ [Qaf: 22], as a rebuke for what they used to do in the world of denying the Resurrection; and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they had been called to prostration while they were sound﴾ [al-Qalam: 43]; and His saying ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21].

The phrase ﴿lakum﴾ (for you) is connected to the verb ﴿kāna﴾ (was), or it is a fixed adverbial phrase occupying the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) relating to ﴿uswatun ḥasanah﴾ (an excellent example).

Abraham, peace be upon him, is a model in certainty in Allah and in zeal for Him. The Arabs, the Jews and the Christians among the nations knew this, and it spread among the neighbouring peoples of the Canaanites and the Aramaeans, and perhaps it reached India. It has been said that the name "Brahma", the deity of the Brahmins among the Hindus, is a corruption of the name Abraham, and this is a possibility.

The phrase ﴿wa-alladhīna maʿahu﴾ (and those with him) is conjoined so that the comparison may be complete: the state of the Muslims with their Messenger ﷺ is likened to the state of Abraham, peace be upon him, and those with him; that is, the Muslims should follow the pleasure of their Messenger ﷺ just as those with Abraham, peace be upon him, did.

What is meant by ﴿alladhīna maʿahu﴾ (those with him) is those who believed in him and followed his guidance, and they were his wife Sarah and his nephew Lot. Abraham had no sons, so the pronoun in ﴿idh qālū﴾ (when they said) refers to Abraham and those with him, and so they were three.

﴿Idh﴾ (when) is a temporal adverb meaning "at the time when", that is: the excellent example is in him and in them at that time.

What is meant by the time is the circumstances occurring within it, which is what the clause that the adverb is attached to explains, namely the clause ﴿they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you"﴾, etc.

The word ﴿uswah﴾ (example) with a kasra or a damma on the hamza is: the model that is followed in some action. It is described in the verse as ﴿ḥasanah﴾ (excellent), a descriptor of praise, because its being excellent is already known from the context of what comes before and after it.

The majority read ﴿iswah﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, while ʿĀṣim read it with a damma. It has been discussed earlier, in His saying ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], in the chapter of al-Ahzab.

The particle ﴿fī﴾ (in) is used metaphorically to express strong association, since it makes the attribution of Abraham and those with him to being an excellent example like the containment of the container by the contained, in the intensity of the qualifying description. For this reason the meaning is: "Abraham and those with him were an example for you at the time of their saying to their people." So His saying ﴿an excellent example in Abraham﴾ is not of the type of tajrīd (abstraction, where a term is detached from its own subject to be attributed to another), like the saying of Abu Khalid al-ʿAttabi:

"And in al-Raḥmān there is a sufficiency for the weak."

Because the example here is the saying of Abraham and those with him, not their persons.

﴿Burāʾ﴾ (free of) with two hamzas, in the pattern of fuʿalāʾ, is the plural of ﴿barīʾ﴾, like ﴿karīm﴾ and ﴿kuramāʾ﴾.

﴿Barīʾ﴾ is of the pattern faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, from "barira", when one becomes free of something, whether after having been in association with it or without any association.

What is meant here is disavowal of their mixing with them and their association with them...

It is conjoined with it: ﴿wa-mā taʿbudūn﴾ (and what you worship), that is, of the idols that you worship besides Allah. And what is meant is: free of worshipping them.

The clause ﴿kafarnā bikum﴾ (we have rejected you) and what is conjoined to it is an explanation of the meaning of the clause ﴿innā burāʾ﴾ (indeed, we are free). The pronoun in ﴿bikum﴾ refers to the totality of the addressees among their people together with what they worship besides Allah. The disbelief is explained by what suits the conjoined element; that is, "we have rejected all of you." Their disbelief in the people is therefore not the same as their disbelief in what their people worship.

Conjoined to it is: ﴿wa-badā baynanā wa-baynakumu al-ʿadāwatu wal-baghḍāʾu abadan﴾ (and enmity and hatred have appeared between us and you forever). The meaning of ﴿badā﴾ is: it became evident and arose, that is: we have brought about enmity with you in a manifest way, with no ambiguity in it. That is, it is not enmity in the heart alone, but is clear enmity, open by speech and by heart. This is the utmost that such as them can do of the degrees of changing the wrong, which is changing it by the tongue, since they are not able to change by hand what their people are upon, due to their small number and weakness among their people.

﴿ʿAdāwah﴾ (enmity) is treating someone with evil and aggression.

﴿Al-baghḍāʾ﴾ (hatred) is the revulsion of the soul and dislike. Each of the two is sometimes used in the place of the other when they are separated. So the mention of both together here is intended to indicate that both states exist in their souls: the state of treating with aggression, and the state of revulsion and dislike. That is, "we will treat you badly and harbour dislike for you until you believe in Allah alone without association."

What is meant by their saying this to their people is that they said it as a speaker of truth in his words. So following them in that saying and in the action that translates what is in the souls upon that saying is: the one imitated in this is that they openly displayed their opposition to their people and declared to them their hatred for the sake of their disbelief in Allah, and did not make compromises with them or overlook their disbelief in order to gain their affection, as the one rebuked in this verse did.

* * *

﴿Except the saying of Abraham to his father: "I will surely seek forgiveness for you, though I have no power to benefit you against Allah at all."﴾

The more apparent view is that this clause is an interjection between the parts of the report of the speech of Abraham and those with him, and the clause ﴿There has certainly been for you in them an excellent example﴾. The exception is disjunctive (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ, an exception not of the same genus as what precedes it), since this saying is not of the same kind as their saying ﴿Indeed, we are free of you﴾, etc. This is because the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely seek forgiveness for you", is gentleness toward his father, and it differs from disavowal of him. So the exception has the meaning of an adversative (istidrāk, a correction introducing a contrast) to His saying ﴿when they said to their people, "Indeed, we are free of you"﴾, which includes the saying of Abraham with them, because the two sayings differ in genus.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf, concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals, except the family of Lot"﴾ [al-Hijr: 58], in the chapter of al-Shuʿara', that it is a disjunctive exception from ﴿qawm﴾ (people), because the people are described as criminals, so the two genera differ on account of that. Thus he made the difference in genus between the excepted and the excepting element the reason for considering the exception disjunctive. The benefit of the adversative here is an allusion to the error of Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿah. That is: if you are making excuses, then let your excuse be in continuing ties with the enemies of Allah by wishing for them forgiveness of their disbelief by seeking the cause of forgiveness, which is that Allah guides them to the true religion, as Abraham said to his father ﴿I will surely seek forgiveness for you﴾. And this cannot be achieved by compromise, by which they do not understand that you are in a place of affection and care toward them, so that they increase in obstinacy in their disbelief.

The reporting of the saying of Abraham to his father ﴿though I have no power to benefit you against Allah at all﴾ completes the statement of what Abraham said to his father, even though the purpose of the exception was merely his promise to seek forgiveness for him. So what is part of his speech was added after it, because it indicates that his seeking forgiveness for him may not be accepted by Allah.

The conjunction ﴿wa﴾ in ﴿wa-mā amliku laka mina Allāhi min shayʾ﴾ may be for a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or for conjunction. The meaning is close, but the circumstantial sense is clearer, and it is a concluding statement (tadhyīl, a closing phrase that sums up the preceding meaning).

The meaning of ownership in His saying ﴿wa-mā amliku﴾ (and I have no power) is power. It has been discussed earlier, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: "Who could prevent Allah if He intended to destroy the Messiah"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], in the chapter of al-ʿUqud.

﴿Min shayʾ﴾ (at all) is general, covering the forgiveness that is requested and other things that Allah wills concerning him.

* * *

﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned in repentance, and to You is the final return.﴾

The more apparent view is that this is part of the speech of Abraham and his people, and the clause ﴿Except the saying of Abraham﴾ up to its end is an interjection between parts of the speech. So it is among the things the Muslims were commanded to imitate, and by it the discourse is very closely connected with His saying ﴿There has certainly been for you in them an excellent example﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 6].

It is possible that it is an instruction to the believers to say this speech and to bring its meanings to mind, so that their actions may be conducted in accordance with it. In that case it is on the assumption of an omitted command to say, and the intended purpose of the speech is acting upon it, since speech renews the meaning in the mind of the one who speaks it and reminds the hearer from his heedlessness. This is a completion of what He instructed them concerning cutting off from the disbelievers, after the exhortation to imitate Abraham and those with him.

According to the first meaning it is a report of what Abraham and his people said, conveying the essential sense of its meanings. Perhaps this is the meaning of what Allah related of Abraham's saying:

﴿Who created me, and He guides me. And who feeds me and gives me drink. And when I am ill, it is He who cures me. And who causes me to die and then gives me life. And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 78–82].

Reliance upon Allah in the affairs of life means asking Him for success in what sets right the servant's works in his endeavours, and the greatest of these is success in his religion, and what it contains of the sustenance of his life, and then what it contains of averting harm. And His saying there, ﴿He is the One who guides me, and who feeds me and gives me drink, and when I am ill, He cures me﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 78–80], gathered them. And this, His saying here, ﴿upon You we have relied﴾, and ﴿And who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 81] is gathered by His saying ﴿and to You is the final return﴾, because the final return is of two kinds: a return after life, and a return after resurrection.

And His saying ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 82]: the means of hope is repentance, and it is contained in His saying ﴿and to You we have turned in repentance﴾.

According to the second meaning, it is an instruction to the believers to direct their attention to Allah by seeking His pleasure, and not to turn to what He does not approve, even if they reckon that they benefit from it, since the pleasure of Allah takes precedence over what is less than it.

The discussion of the meaning of reliance (tawakkul) was given earlier, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when you have made a decision, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al ʿImran: 159], in the chapter of Al ʿImran.

Repentance (inābah) means turning back in repentance, and it was given earlier, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed Abraham was forbearing, grieving, and turning back in repentance﴾ [Hud: 75], in the chapter of Hud, and at His saying ﴿turning back in repentance to Him﴾ [al-Rum: 31], in the chapter of al-Rum.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before these verbs is for the purpose of restriction (qaṣr, limiting the action to the object), and it is a restriction that is partly claimed (idiʿāʾī, rhetorically asserted) and partly real, as the context directs.

The repetition of the address with their saying ﴿Our Lord﴾ is a display of humble supplication with each of the three invocations.

[Page 148]

**Fitnah** (trial, affliction, turmoil): the disruption and corruption of a state of affairs. It is an ism masdar (a noun of verbal action, used as a verbal noun), so it may be used in the sense of the verbal noun, as in His saying ﴿and persecution is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], and it may be used as a descriptive term for the one who is afflicted and for the one who afflicts.

The meaning of "making them a trial for those who disbelieve" is: making them afflicted, such that those who disbelieve afflict them. This is confirmed in that those who disbelieve gain power over them and they are persecuted, as He said, ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], and so on. It is also confirmed in that the affairs of their religion are thrown into disorder because of those who disbelieve, that is, through their love for them and their drawing close to them, as in His saying, relating the supplication of Musa, ﴿It is none but Your trial; You send astray by it whom You will﴾ [al-A'raf: 155].

On both interpretations, fitnah is used as an ism masdar in the sense of an ism maf'ul (passive participle). It was previously discussed in His saying ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ [Yunus: 85], in Surat Yunus.

The lam in ﴿for those who disbelieve﴾ is, on both interpretations, the lam of ownership, meaning: afflicted, subjugated to them.

In my view, it is also permissible that fitnah be a masdar in the sense of an ism al-fa'il (active participle), meaning: "Do not make us persecutors," that is, a cause of trial for those who disbelieve. This becomes a kinayah (metonymy) for the meaning: do not let those who disbelieve prevail over us, and turn away from us whatever would cause the disruption of our affair and the evil of our conditions, so that none of that becomes a trial for those who disbelieve, that is, one that strengthens their trial, so that they are tested in their religion, that is, they increase in disbelief. This is a trial in religion, meaning they would suppose that we are upon falsehood and that they are upon the truth. Fitnah is also sometimes used for what leads to deception in religion, as in His saying, ﴿Rather, it is a trial﴾ [al-Zumar: 49] in Surat al-Zumar, and His saying, ﴿I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and an enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-Anbiya': 111] in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The lam on this interpretation is the lam of tabligh (conveyance, i.e., the lam that marks the one to whom something is communicated or directed). These are many meanings which this verse has conveyed.

* * *

﴿And forgive us, our Lord﴾: after their supplications which return to the reform of their religion in this world, they follow them with a request for what will reform their affairs in the Hereafter, and for what brings about the pleasure of Allah with them in this world. For His pleasure leads to His care for them, by facilitating their affairs in both lives. The conjunction "and" (wa) is used here to indicate the difference between the two supplications, so it is connected, whereas the earlier one was not connected to what preceded it.

* * *

﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾.

[Page 149]

This is a justification (ta'lil) for all the supplications. Reliance upon Him, turning to Him in repentance, and the return to Him are suited to the attribute of the Exalted in Might, since one of such might treats others in a like manner. Their request that He not make them a trial is, in its various meanings, suited to the attribute of the Wise. Likewise, their request for forgiveness: when they pleaded to Him that He not make them a trial for the disbelievers, and that He forgive them, they saw that His wisdom would be suited to answering their supplication, because it contains their well-being, and they had come asking Him.

﴿There has certainly been for you in them an excellent example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾

This repeats His earlier statement, ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4], and so on. It is repeated to emphasize the exhortation and urging not to neglect following their example, and so that His statement ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ and what follows can be built upon it.

He joined this emphasis with the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) for greater emphasis. The feminine ta' (تاء التأنيث) did not attach to the verb kāna even though its subject (ism) is feminine in form, because the feminine gender of ʾuswah is not real (ḥaqīqī), and because a separation occurred between the verb and its subject by the prepositional phrase and its object.

The ʾuswah (example) is the one mentioned before, and the readers differed over its hamzah in His statement ﴿There has certainly been for you an excellent example﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4].

His statement ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ is a badal (substitution, apposition: "badal") for the pronoun of address in His statement "for you" (lakum). It includes all those addressed, because those addressed by the pronoun lakum are the believers in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1]. So the mention of ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾ is not a restriction to some of the believers; rather it is a reminder that belief in Allah and the Last Day requires that they follow the earlier believers, namely Ibrahim and those with him.

The preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) that governs the substituted term was repeated to emphasize that belief necessitates that.

The purpose is to increase the urging to follow Ibrahim and those with him, and so that His statement ﴿And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾ follows from it. This is a warning against returning to what they were forbidden.

[Page 150]

The verb yatawalla is the present tense of tawallā. Its past form may mean "turning away," i.e., whoever does not hope for Allah and the Last Day and turns away from the prohibition of Allah, then Allah is Free of need from his obedience. In my view it may also be from tawallī in the sense of "taking an ally," i.e., whoever takes the enemy of Allah as allies, then Allah is Free of need of his alliance, as in His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], in the Surah of al-ʿUqūd.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) in His statement "He is the Free of need" (huwa al-Ghaniyy) is an emphasis of the restriction (ḥaṣr) conveyed by the definiteness of the two components. It is a claimed restriction (ḥaṣr iddiʿāʾī), meaning that the independence of others and their praise are not taken into account; that is, He is Free of need of those who turn away, because the prohibition of what they were forbidden is only for their own benefit and does not benefit Allah in any way. He is therefore Free of need of everything.

Following "the Free of need" (al-Ghaniyy) with the description "the Praiseworthy" (al-Ḥamīd) is a tatmīm (completion, supplementation), meaning: the Praiseworthy to whoever obeys His command and does not turn away from it, or the Praiseworthy to whoever does not take His enemy as an ally, in the manner of His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is Free of need of you; and He does not approve disbelief for His servants. And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7].

**Translation:**

This is an *i'tiraḍ* (interjected clause, a parenthetical that breaks into the discourse) and an *isti'nāf* (a resumptive clause) that is connected to what precedes it from the beginning of the surah. It is addressed to the believers as consolation for what they were forbidden of maintaining ties with their relatives. They are told to hope from God that He will turn their severance into affection, by bringing the polytheists out of their kinship with the believers. God has indeed fulfilled this on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, through the Islam of Abū Sufyān, al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, and Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Among this affection was the Prophet's (ﷺ) marriage to Umm Ḥabība bint Abī Sufyān. He married her after the death of her husband ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaḥsh in the land of Abyssinia (Ḥabasha), after her husband had become a Christian. When the Prophet (ﷺ) married her, Abū Sufyān's stubbornness softened, and he openly acknowledged the Prophet's (ﷺ) excellence, saying: (That stallion's nose will not be struck). It is narrated with a *dāl* after the *qāf*, from *qada'a*, meaning: when he struck its nose with a spear. This is a metaphor. When an ignoble stallion mounted a noble she-camel, they would push him away from her by striking his nose with a spear, so that her offspring would not be a *hajīn* (a mongrel, of inferior stock).

Given that it has been established that this surah was revealed in the year of the Conquest of Mecca, and that the Prophet's (ﷺ) marriage to Umm Ḥabība took place during her emigration to Abyssinia, which was before the Conquest of Mecca, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others have stated, this means that the verse "﴿ʿAsā Allāh an yajʿala baynakum﴾" and so on was revealed before the beginning of the surah and was then appended to it.

Alternatively, Ibn ʿAbbās's statement may be meant as an example of the affection that arises with some of the polytheists, and the arising of such affection prepares its bearer for Islam. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, however, considered the authenticity of what was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās to be doubtful.

*ʿAsā* is a verb of approximation (*fiʿl muqārabah*). Here it is used to express the believers' hope from God, or it is used to express a promise, stripped of the sense of hope. In the *Kashshāf* it is said: "Just as a king says regarding some needs, ʿasā or laʿalla, so that the one in need has no doubt about its fulfillment."

The pronoun in "﴿minhum﴾" refers to the enemy mentioned in His words: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah: 1]. The clause "﴿wa-Llāhu qadīr﴾" is a *tadhyīl* (a concluding clause that generalizes the preceding statement). The meaning is: He is entirely capable of changing circumstances so that the polytheists become sincere believers and you become their friends.

The clause "﴿wa-Llāhu ghafūrun raḥīm﴾" is joined to the concluding clause. That is, He forgives those who turn back to Him and has mercy upon them. Thus there is no wonder that they should become your friends, just as you become their friends.

[p. 151]

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on surah 60, verse 8:

﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of your religion and do not expel you from your homes, from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them. Indeed, God loves the just.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a sentence that opens a new clause) which states explicitly what is implied by the attributes used to describe the enemy in His words ﴿And they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth, expelling the Messenger and yourselves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and His words ﴿If they gain control over you, they will be enemies to you and extend against you their hands and their tongues with evil﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2]. These are presented as the justification for the prohibition on taking the enemies of God as allies. God makes an exception for groups among the polytheists who did not harbor enmity toward the Muslims, and whose religion was strongly opposed to the religion of Islam.

If we consider the description of the enemy in His words ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], and understand it as applying to the state of opposing those who differ with them in religion, and we also consider the description ﴿they expel the Messenger and yourselves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], then the content of His words ﴿God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion,﴾ through to the end of the verse, is an explanation of the meaning of the enmity that is made the cause for the prohibition on allegiance. The meaning would then be that the basis of the prohibition is the totality of the attributes mentioned, with each attribute taken on its own.

If we consider that the description of the enemy is "the enemy of the religion," meaning one who opposes it in himself, together with the added description ﴿And they have disbelieved in what has come to you of the truth﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], then the content of ﴿God does not forbid you﴾ through to the end of the verse specifies the prohibition to the particular enemies of the religion who did not fight the Muslims for the sake of religion and did not expel the Muslims from their homes.

In any case, this sentence has excluded from the ruling of prohibition the people who did not fight over religion and did not expel the Muslims from their homes. The connection of this verse with the verses before it makes the two considerations equal. Thus, within the ruling of the verse there entered categories of people, namely the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Khuza'ah, the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b ibn 'Abd Manat ibn Kinanah, and Muzaynah. All of these were supporters of the Prophet (ﷺ) and wished for his victory over the Quraysh. Also included were the women and children among the polytheists. Qutaylah (diminutive form; she is also called Qatilah, in the augmented form), daughter of 'Abd al-'Uzza, from the Banu 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy of the Quraysh, who was the mother of Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, came to Madinah visiting her daughter, while Qutaylah was then a polytheist, during the period of truce between the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the disbelievers of the Quraysh after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, the period during which this surah was revealed. Asma' asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Should I maintain ties with my mother?" He said: "Yes, maintain ties with your mother." It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning her.

His words ﴿from being righteous toward them﴾ are a comprehensive substitution (*badal al-ishtimal*, a substitute that encompasses the original term in meaning) for ﴿those who do not fight you because of religion﴾, etc. This is because the presence of a pronoun referring back to the relative clause in the substituted element, namely the object pronoun in ﴿that you be righteous toward them﴾, makes the Muslims' righteousness toward them one of the things their circumstances include. Thus there entered among those who did not fight the Muslims over religion a group from the Banu Hashim, among them al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. All those whom the rulings of this verse encompass, it has been said, were the cause of its revelation, but it is only a general inclusion and not a cause of revelation.

Al-birr (righteousness) means good treatment and honoring. It takes a prepositional complement, as one says *barra bihi*, but its transitivity here is directly, by dropping the preposition.

Al-qist means justice. The verb *tuqsitu* has been given the sense of *tufdu* (to go out to, to reach), so it takes *ila* (to). Its original construction should have been with *li*. However, *li* and *ila* often substitute for each other in speech. The meaning is: that you treat them in the same manner in which they treat you with kindness, for treating someone in the same way he has treated you is justice.

The clause ﴿Indeed, God loves the just﴾ is a concluding summary (*tadhyil*), meaning that He loves every just person. Thus those who act justly toward those who are their allies in religion enter into it, when they are opposed in belief yet treat them well.

From Ibn Wahb, who said: I asked Ibn Zayd about His words ﴿God does not forbid you﴾ through to the end of the verse, and he said: "Fighting abrogated it." Al-Tabari said: There is no basis for the view of those who say that this is abrogated, because the righteousness of believers toward those who are related to them among the people of war, or toward those with whom there is no kinship but who are not forbidden to them, is permissible when it contains no indication of a weakness of the people of Islam. End quote.

From this verse is derived the permissibility of treating the protected people (*ahl al-dhimmah*) with kindness, and the permissibility of showing courtesy toward them personally.

Summary of the preceding discussion and restriction of the ruling of the previous verse. It indicates the end of the purpose for which the speech was delivered from its beginning.

The restriction (qasr) derived from the phrase ﴿Indeed, Allah only forbids you from those who fight you over religion and expel you from your homes and aid in your expulsion, that you make allies of them﴾ to its end is a reversed restriction (qasr maqlub), meant to refute the belief of someone who supposed or doubted the permissibility of befriending the polytheists in general. Those in whom these attributes were realized on the day of the revelation of the verse are the polytheists of Makkah, and ﴿that you make allies of them﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from ﴿those who fight you﴾.

﴿And whoever makes allies of them﴾ is a conditional clause, and the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) was used in the answer of the condition to distinguish those being pointed to, for additional clarity of the ruling.

Al-muzaharah (zahir, "aid") means assistance. This is because the people of Makkah were of two groups: among them were those who brought about the circumstances that made it impossible for the Muslims to remain in Makkah, and among them were those who assisted in that and incited toward it.

The restriction derived from His saying ﴿Then it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ is a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i), meaning that their wrongdoing, because of its severity and its occurrence after the strong prohibition and the warning about the transgressions and disobedience, is a wrongdoing that is not forgiven, because it is an aggression upon the rights of Allah and the rights of the Muslims, and upon the right of the wrongdoer himself.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 10 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, then test them. Allah is most knowing of their faith. And if you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful [wives] for the disbelievers, nor are the disbelievers lawful [husbands] for them.﴾

There is no disagreement that these verses at the end of the surah were revealed after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah. You have already learned that we preferred the view that the beginning of the surah was revealed before these verses, and that the letter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to the polytheists was written while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was preparing for al-Hudaybiyah.

The occasion for the revelation of this verse after what precedes it, namely the prohibition of allying with the polytheists, is that this prohibition extends to the marriage bonds and affinity (musahara) between Muslims and polytheists. A Muslim man may be married to a polytheist woman, and a Muslim woman may be married to a polytheist man, and events arise concerning this that the Muslims cannot do without knowing the ruling of the Sharia on their like.

After the treaty that was concluded between the Prophet ﷺ and the polytheists at al-Hudaybiyah in the sixth year [AH], there occurred the arrival of Abu Jandal ibn 'Amr, dragging his feet in iron shackles. He was a Muslim, bound in chains by his father in Makkah. He escaped and came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was at al-Hudaybiyah. Among the conditions of the treaty was that whoever came to Muhammad from Quraysh without the permission of his guardian, he would be returned to them, and whoever came to Quraysh from those who were with Muhammad, they would not return him to him. So the Prophet ﷺ returned him to them.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah, Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt emigrated, fleeing from her husband 'Amr ibn al-'As. Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah came as an emigrant, fleeing from her husband Safi ibn al-Rahib, or Musafir al-Makhzumi. Umaymah bint Bishr came, fleeing from her husband Thabit ibn al-Shimrakh, or it is said: Hassan ibn al-Dahdah. Their husbands sought them. Some of them came to Madinah. The husband of Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah came seeking her return to him, and he said: "The clay of the document between us and you has not yet dried." Then this verse was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ refused to return her to him, and he returned none of them to them. They remained in Madinah. Zayd ibn Harithah married Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah; Sahl ibn Hunayf married Subay'ah; and Sahl ibn Hunayf married Umaymah.

Zaynab, the daughter of the Prophet ﷺ, came as a Muslim, and her husband Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi' ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza followed her after years, while he was still a polytheist. Then he embraced Islam in Madinah, and the Prophet ﷺ returned her to him.

There is a difference of opinion: was the prohibition concerning believing women emigrants, that they should not be returned to the disbelievers, an abrogation (naskh, abrogation of an earlier ruling) of what the treaty between the Prophet ﷺ and the polytheists contained? Or was the treaty not explicit about returning women, because the wording was in the masculine plural form, and so it was regarded as general (mujmal), and the prohibition in this verse was an explanation of that generality? It has also been said that the treaty was explicit that whoever came to the Prophet ﷺ without the permission of his guardian, whether man or woman, would be returned to his guardian. If that is established, then it was explicit, and the verse was an abrogation (naskh) of what the Prophet ﷺ had done.

What is in the Sira of Ibn Ishaq, in the transmission of Ibn Hisham, is free of this explicit statement. Therefore the wording of the treaty was open to the meaning of men only, because the pronouns it included were masculine pronouns.

It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to those who asked him to return the believing women and demanded the implementation of the treaty's conditions: "The condition applies to men, not to women." So this verse was legislation for the Muslims regarding what they should do when believing women come to them as emigrants, and a notice to the polytheists that their condition was not explicit. The nature of treaty conditions is that they should be explicit, because of the gravity of concluded agreements and the rights that follow from them. Allah distracted the polytheists from taking precaution in their condition, so that this would be a mercy to the emigrant women, since He made a way out for them, and a support for His Messenger ﷺ, as in the verse that follows, with the aim that those among the believers who are able to ascertain the sincerity of the faith of the emigrant women should join in cooperating to uphold the truth. Also, much of the obligation contained in it relates to the circumstances of believing men with their women.

[Page 156]

*Al-imtihan* means testing, examination. What is meant is testing their faith.

The clause ﴿Allah is most knowing of their faith﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah), meaning that Allah knows their inner states, but you must test this by whatever indicators you can.

On that basis, He built upon what came before the parenthesis with His words ﴿And if you know them to be believers﴾ and so on, meaning: if you come to have knowledge that they are believers, not lying in their claim. This joining (iltihaq) is what is called the pledge (mubaya'ah) in His words in the following verse: ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you, that they will not associate anything with Allah﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12], and so on.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is narrated from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to test those women emigrants who came with this verse, saying: Allah said, ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12] until His words ﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12]. Ibn 'Abbas added: "The test was that she would be made to swear that she had not left out of hatred for her husband, nor out of desire to move from one land to another, nor seeking worldly gain, nor out of love for a man among us, nor because of a fault she had committed, but out of love for Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter. When she swore by Allah, besides whom there is no god, that this was so, the Prophet ﷺ would give her husband her dowry and what he had spent on her, and he would not return her. The Prophet ﷺ used to command 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to take charge of making them swear. When a woman's faith became clear, the Prophet ﷺ did not return her to the abode of disbelief," as is the plain meaning of the verse. ﴿So do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful [wives] for them, nor are they lawful [husbands] for them.﴾

The placement of His words ﴿They are not lawful [wives] for them, nor are they lawful [husbands] for them﴾ is that of explanation and elaboration of the prohibition in His words ﴿So do not return them to the disbelievers﴾, confirming the obligation of separation between the believing woman and her disbelieving husband.

Since the one addressed by that prohibition was all the believers, as the wording ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you﴾ to its end requires, it became necessary that the one who carries out its implementation be the one charged with the general affairs of the Muslims in every place and every time, namely the rulers of affairs, such as commanders and judges. For it is not possible for the Muslims to carry out what they were addressed with, regarding general matters of this kind, except in this manner. But each individual Muslim is obliged to act upon it in his own person, and to comply with what the rulers of affairs decide.

[Page 157]

Since the sense of the word *hill* (lawfulness) and its derivations, in the speech of the Lawgiver, refers to the legal permissibility (ibahah shar'iyyah), which is permission and the opposite of prohibition,

it is clear that disbelievers are not addressed with the obligations of Islamic law, since they are outside it. So demanding that they fulfil Islamic obligations is not connected to the purpose of the Sharia. For this reason, the question known in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence) as "the address of disbelievers with the subsidiary rulings" is regarded as a matter of no benefit, and one should not occupy oneself with it, let alone build rulings upon it.

Since the ruling denying the woman's lawfulness (hill), which is the meaning of the prohibition of the continuation of her marital bond, was attached in His words ﴿They are not lawful [wives] for them﴾ to the pronoun of the disbelievers, and since disbelievers are not fit for being addressed with this prohibition, the interpretation of this prohibition must be understood in relation to its being upon the disbelievers. This is done by attributing the negated quality of *hill* to the women in both clauses, and by showing the reason for the arrangement of the two clauses and the reversal in the order of their parts. This means we say: the return of the believing woman to a disbeliever occurs in two forms.

One: that the believing woman returns to her husband in the land of disbelief. This is what the disbelievers insisted on demanding when some believing women came as emigrants.

The second: that she returns to her husband in the land of Islam, by leaving her free to be with her disbelieving husband, who stays with her in the land of Islam when he comes seeking her and is prevented from taking her. Both forms are unlawful for the Muslim woman, so the rulers of affairs do not permit them. The first form is expressed by the clause ﴿They are not lawful [wives] for them﴾, in which the attribute *hill* (lawful) is made a predicate of the pronoun of the women, and the preposition *lam* is attached to the pronoun of the men. This *lam* denotes transitivity of *hill*, and its original sense is the *lam* of ownership. Thus it conveys that disbelieving men do not own the marital bond of their believing wives. This implies that the continuation of believing women in the marital bond of their disbelieving husbands is unlawful, meaning that Islam has not made them lawful to those men.

The clause ﴿They are not lawful [wives] for them﴾ was placed first because it refers to the form that was more important to the polytheists, since they were seeking the return of the women and sending intermediaries for this purpose, aiming to have them returned by this means.

In the first clause the attributive adjective *hill* (lawful), which indicates the established quality, was used,

[Page 158]

since the disbelieving men thought that the marital authority they held over their believing wives established that the women were lawful to them.

The second clause, ﴿nor are they lawful [husbands] for them﴾, expresses the second form. The predication of *hill* was reversed: it was made a predicate of the pronoun of the men, and the verb was transitivized to the one made lawful by means of the *lam* attached to the pronoun of the women. This conveys that their disbelieving husbands are not lawful for them, even if the husband remains in the land of Islam.

For this reason the second clause, ﴿nor are they lawful [husbands] for them﴾, is mentioned as a completion of the ruling of the first clause. In the second clause the predicate was a present-tense verb, because it indicates renewal, to convey the negation of the expectation of making lawful, even if it were renewed in the present by a new contract or a new agreement to remain in the land of Islam. This is contrary to Abu Hanifah, who said: the cause of separation is the difference of the two lands, not the difference of religion.

There is another possible sense of the verse: that the purpose is to emphasize the negation in the present. After saying ﴿They are not lawful [wives] for them﴾, which is the basic statement, as you have learned just now, it is emphasized by the clause ﴿nor are they lawful [husbands] for them﴾, meaning that the negation of lawfulness is established from every direction, as one says: "You are not of me, and I am not of you."

A parallel to this is His words ﴿They are garments for you, and you are garments for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187] in Surah al-Baqarah, as an emphasis on the intensity of mutual enveloping and closeness from every direction.

In the speech there is also the rhetorical embellishment of *al-'aks* (chiasmus, reversal), one of the decorative figures of rhetoric, with a slight change between *hill* and *yahillun*, which the context required. The share of embellishment is given only to the degree that the requirement of eloquence permits.

The majority of reciters read ﴿wa la tumsikū﴾ with a damma on the ta', a sukun on the mim, and a kasra on the sin, lightened (tumsikū). Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the mim, and a kasra on the sin with shadda, as the present tense of massaka, meaning amsaka (to hold).

﴿And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ is conjoined to God's words ﴿and give them what they have spent﴾, and it completes its ruling. This is equity between the two parties, and the command is one of permission (ibaha).

His words ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ complete his words ﴿and ask for what you have spent﴾, to indicate that the meaning of the conjunctive waw here is simultaneity (al-ma'iyya), by the context. For if His words ﴿and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ were meant to have their ruling alone, then His words ﴿and give them what they have spent﴾ would have sufficed in its place. So the waw conveys the meaning of simultaneity here by the context. What some of the Hanafis have said should be understood in this sense, that the meaning of the conjunctive waw is simultaneity.
