These rulings in these verses concerning the exchange of dowries were legislated for specific circumstances, required by the mixing of affairs between the people of polytheism and the believers, and the treaty of truce between the Muslims and the polytheists at the beginning of Islam was specific to that time, by the consensus of the scholars. This was stated by Ibn al-'Arabi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Bakr al-Jassas.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 11:

﴿And if any of your wives escape you to the disbelievers, and then you have a turn [of gain], give to those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent. And fear God, in whom you are believers.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) to the clause ﴿And ask for what you have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], for when the refusal of the polytheists to return the dowries of women who remained in disbelief in Mecca, and of those who fled from Medina and joined the people of disbelief in Mecca, followed from its revelation, this verse was appended to legislate the return of those dowries from the property of the Muslims among themselves.

It is narrated that the Muslims wrote to the polytheists informing them of what this verse contained of the mutual restitution between the two parties, in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And ask for what you have spent, and let them ask for what they have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10].

The polytheists refused to pay the dowries of the women who had gone over to them, so He, Exalted is He, revealed ﴿And if any of your wives escape you to the disbelievers﴾, and the verse.

The root of al-fawt (escape, loss) is separation and distancing, and al-tafawut is distance. Al-fawt here is used figuratively for the loss of a right, as in the verse of Ruwaysh ibn Kathir al-Ta'i or 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"If you commit sins, then your remnant come to me, there is no sin of yours upon me that is a loss (fawt)."

That is: there is no loss upon me by what you have sinned, meaning: we are like one whose right has not been lost.

The meaning is: if some of your wives flee and join the disbelievers, and there occurs a reciprocity between you and the disbelievers, so that you have a turn over the wives of the disbelievers and the disbelievers have a turn over your wives, and the disbelievers refuse to pay the dowries of some of the women who went to them, then you should pay to the one whom the disbelievers have deprived of the dowry of his wife, that is, what is his due, and withhold that from the disbelievers. This implies that if all the believers are given the dowries of those whose wives escaped from them, and a surplus remains with the polytheists, the Muslims return it to the disbelievers. This is the explanation of al-Zuhri in the transmission of Yunus from him, and it is the most apparent of what the verse has been explained by.

From Ibn 'Abbas and the majority: those whose wives escaped to the disbelievers are given the dowries of their women from the spoils of the Muslims. This implies that the verse is abrogated by the verse of Surah Bara'ah: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7].

The preferable view is that one does not resort to giving from the spoils except when there is nothing owed by the Muslims of the dowries of the wives of the polytheists who came to the lands of Islam and became wives of the Muslims.

The speech is a highly elliptical concision (ijaz hadhf shadid), indicated by the totality of the words, and the place of the speech is after His saying, ﴿And if any of your wives escape you﴾.

The word (shay') here is meant as: some of ﴿your wives﴾, the clarification of (shay'). And (shay') is intended to demean the wives who refused Islam, for the intended sense is that their very persons have escaped from their husbands, so there is no benefit to him in them.

The verb (fatakum) is used with the sense of flight, so it takes the preposition (ila), that is, they fled to the disbelievers.

(ʿAqqabtum) is the form tafa'ala from al-ʿuqba (with a damma on the ʿayn and a sukun on the qaf), which is the turn, that is, one's coming to a state in which another had been. Its origin is in riding mounts and beasts, where one rides a stage and another a stage; the ruling applied to the two parties, namely these paying the dowries of those women in some circumstances and those paying the dowries of these women in other similar circumstances, is likened to a mount they take turns on.

Thus the verb (dhahabat) is metaphorical, like the verb (fatakum), in the sense of lack of power over them.

The address in His saying ﴿And if any of your wives escape you﴾ and in His saying ﴿give﴾ is addressed to the believers, and those whose wives went away are also among the believers.

The meaning: let the believers give to their brothers whose wives went away what is equal to the dowries they had given their wives.

The one who undertakes the giving here, as we established in His saying ﴿and give them what they have spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], is that it is paid from the property of the Muslims, such as the spoils and the fifths and the like, as the Sunnah has explained: the Prophet ﷺ gave ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, ʿIyad ibn Abi Shaddad al-Fihri, Shammas ibn ʿUthman, and Hisham ibn al-ʿAs the dowries of their women who had joined the polytheists, from the spoils.

The word (mithl), "the like," indicates that the dowry given should be equal to what the woman's husband had previously given, without any deficiency.

The verse refers to some women of the emigrants who did not embrace Islam, and they were eight women: Umm al-Hakam bint Abi Sufyan, who was under ʿIyad ibn Shaddad; Fatimah bint Abi Umayyah, also called Qurayba, who was the sister of Umm Salamah, and who was under ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab; Umm Kulthum bint Jarwal, who was under ʿUmar; Baroʿ, with a fatha on the ba' according to the more correct view (the traditionists pronounce it with a kasra), daughter of ʿUqba, who was under Shammas ibn ʿUthman; Shahbah bint Ghaylan; ʿAbdah bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzza, who was under Hisham ibn al-ʿAs, and it is said under ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd; Hind bint Abi Jahl, who was under Hisham ibn al-ʿAs; and Arwa bint Rabiʿa ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, who was under Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah. He had emigrated, and his wife remained a polytheist in Mecca, so when the verse was revealed, Talhah ibn ʿUbaydullah divorced her.

It has preceded that ʿUmar divorced his two wives Qurayba and Umm Jarwal, so they were not among those who joined the polytheists; rather, they remained in Mecca until ʿUmar divorced them. I suppose that all of them were divorced by their husbands at the revelation of His saying, ﴿And do not hold on to the marriage bonds of disbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10].

The concluding phrase ﴿And fear God, in whom you are believers﴾ is an exhortation to the Muslims to fulfil what God has commanded them, and not to let the injustice and lack of equity of the polytheists toward them prevent them from fulfilling part of it. So He commanded that the Muslims pay their brothers the dowries of the women whom they had separated from, and whose dowries the polytheists did not agree to give; for this reason the divine name was followed by the description ﴿in whom you are believers﴾, because faith impels toward piety, and since the polytheists did not believe in what God commanded, the restraint of equity was absent from them, that is, do not be like them.

The nominal clause within the relative clause indicates the firmness of their faith.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 12:

﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill their children, nor bring forth a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet, nor disobey you in what is right, then accept their pledge and ask God's forgiveness for them. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

This is a continuation of the examination of women mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants, then examine them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], and an explanation of the details of its consequences. It is as if He is saying: If you know them to be believers, then do not return them to the disbelievers, and explain to them the laws of Islam. The verse of examination came after the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, concerning those women who emigrated from Makkah to Madinah after the treaty. They were: Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, Sabay'a al-Aslamiyya, Umaymah bint Bishr, and Zaynab bint Rasul Allah (ﷺ). Therefore there is no validity to the reports which claim that the verse was revealed at the conquest of Makkah; their origin is confusion in events and the mixing up of what was repeated with what was previously mentioned.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from 'A'isha that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to examine the women who emigrated, with this verse (﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾) up to His words (﴿Forgiving, Merciful﴾). Whoever among the women acknowledged this condition, the Messenger of God would say to her: "I have accepted your pledge."

The implication of this pledge after the examination is that they had entered Islam after the rulings of the religion had become established over a period of years, during which they had not witnessed what the men had witnessed of the gradual expansion of legislation. For this reason this pledge began with the emigrant women, as indicated by His words ﴿when believing women come to you﴾, meaning they came to you from Makkah. It is thus parallel to His words ﴿O you who have believed, when believing women come to you as emigrants﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This pledge took place on the second day of the Conquest, at the Mount Safa.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also applied this pledge to the women of the Ansar. Al-Bukhari narrated from Umm 'Atiyya, who said: "We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he recited to us ﴿that they will not associate anything with God﴾," and the hadith continues.

Also in it, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I attended the Eid al-Fitr prayer with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before the sermon. The Prophet of God descended, and it is as if I am looking at him as he seats the men with his hand. Then he moved along them, pushing through, until he came to the women with Bilal, and he said: (﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you that they will not associate﴾), until he finished the whole verse. Then when he finished, he said: 'Are you upon that?' A woman among them, alone, whom no one else answered, said: 'Yes, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'Then give charity.'"

He also applied this pledge to the men. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Will you pledge allegiance to me that you will not associate anything with God, nor commit theft, nor adultery,' and he recited the verse of the women (that is, the one revealed in address to women in surah al-Mumtahanah). Whoever among you fulfills it, his reward is with God. Whoever commits any of that and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him. Whoever commits some of it and God conceals it, then it is up to God: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him."

The practice of this pledge continued until the day of the Conquest of Makkah, when its people had embraced Islam, men and women. On the second day of the Conquest he sat at al-Safa taking the pledge from the men according to what is in this verse, [Page 166] and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab sat taking the pledge from the women according to that. Among the women who pledged to him that day were Hind bint 'Utba, wife of Abu Sufyan, and Kabsha bint Rafi'.

The clause ﴿they pledge allegiance to you﴾ may be a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, al-ḥāl, a grammatical state describing the subject at the time of the action) from "the believing women," meaning: "they desire the pledge," which is the one mentioned in this verse. The answer of the conditional (idhā) is ﴿then accept their pledge﴾.

It may also be that the clause "they pledge allegiance to you" is the answer of the conditional (idhā).

The meaning of ﴿when believing women come to you﴾ is: those who have entered the community of believers in general and in summary, not knowing the principles of Islam; and He explained this by His words ﴿they pledge allegiance to you﴾. So it is a statement (khabar) intended as a command (amr), meaning: "let them pledge allegiance to you." The clause ﴿then accept their pledge﴾ is a consequence (tafrī') of the clause ﴿they pledge allegiance to you﴾, and upon it is built His words ﴿and ask God's forgiveness for them﴾.

The verse includes abandonment of certain traits of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period of ignorance). Theft was more common among women than among men. A Bedouin said when his wife gave birth to a daughter: "By God, she is not a good child: her crying is a plague and her help is theft."

The killing of children has two meanings: the first is wa'd (burying infant daughters alive), which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do to their daughters; the second is the expulsion of fetuses, which is abortion.

The killing is attributed to women, although some of it is done by men, because women used to consent to it or remain silent about it.

Buhtan (slander) is a false report about which the one who fabricates it has no pretext, because it confounds (yabhutu) the one about whom it is transmitted.

Iftira' (fabrication) is the inventing of falsehood, meaning: they should not invent reports about things that did not happen.

His words ﴿between their hands and their feet﴾ are connected to (ya'tīna, "they bring forth"). This is an expression comprehensive of many meanings according to its various interpretations, whether literal, figurative, or metonymic. The literal meaning of buhtan is the report of a falsehood, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The verbal noun is sometimes used in the sense of the passive participle, as khalq (creation) means "the created thing."

The literal meaning of "between the hands and the feet" is that the lie occurs in a place lying between the hands and the feet. If buhtan is taken in its literal sense, namely a false report, then its fabrication "between their hands and their feet" means that she lies openly in the face of the one she accuses, as in her saying: "O so-and-so, you committed adultery with so-and-so," or "You stole the jewelry of so-and-so," in order to confound her in front of people, or "You are the child of adultery," or something similar.

If buhtan is taken in the sense of the thing falsely reported, then the meaning of fabricating it "between their hands and their feet" is a metonymy for the claim of pregnancy: that she drinks something that inflates her belly, so that she makes her husband think she is pregnant; then she displays labor pains and brings forth a child she has picked up and attributes to her husband, so that he will not divorce her or so that his male relatives will not inherit from him. She enlarges her belly while it is before her, then when the time of displaying labor comes she places the infant between her legs, and people talk about it, and so it is the thing falsely reported (mabhūt 'alayhi). Thus fabrication (iftira') is her claim of that, as an emphasis on the meaning of buhtan.

If buhtan is used figuratively for falsehood resembling a false report, then ﴿between their hands and their feet﴾ may be a metonymy for a woman giving herself to someone other than her husband, who kisses her or touches her, which is "between their hands," or who commits adultery with her, which is "between their feet."

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani interpreted it as sorcery, since she handles its matters with her hands while sitting, placing the items of sorcery between her legs.

These interpretations do not preclude the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) took the pledge of the men with something similar. Some of these interpretations cannot be imagined for men, since each category takes what suits it from among them.

After singling out these prohibited matters for mention because of the gravity of their concern, he generalized the prohibition with His words ﴿nor disobey you in what is right﴾. Ma'ruf (what is right) is that which souls do not reject. Here it means what is right in religion. Restricting it to this is either merely for clarification, since the Prophet (ﷺ) only commands what is right, or it is for the purpose of granting them latitude in a matter not connected to religion, as Barira did when she refused the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ) to return to her husband Mughith after she was separated from him by her manumission while he was a slave.

It has been narrated in the Sahih from Umm 'Atiyya that the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them in this pledge from wailing (niyaha), so a woman withdrew her hand and said: "So-and-so helped me, and I want to repay her." The Prophet (ﷺ) said nothing to her, so she left and came back, and he accepted her pledge. This is only an example of some of what is right which the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them, the neglect of which was widespread among them.

It is reported in narrations that he forbade them from the display of adornment (tabarruj) of the Jahiliyyah and from speaking to men who were not mahram (those they may never marry). 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "O Prophet of God, we have guests, and we are often absent." The Messenger of God said: "It is not them that I meant."

From Ibn 'Abbas: he forbade them from tearing garments, scratching faces, cutting hair, and calling out for destruction and loss, meaning among the matters of wailing in the Jahiliyyah.

Al-Tabari narrated with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the pledge from the women, Hind bint 'Utba, wife of Abu Sufyan, was sitting with the women, disguised out of fear of the Messenger of God, lest he retaliate against her for slitting open the belly of Hamza and removing his liver on the day of Uhud. When he said: 'that they will not associate anything with God,' Hind said: 'How can we hope that He will accept from us anything He did not accept from the men?' When he said: 'nor steal,' Hind said: 'By God, I take some of Abu Sufyan's wealth, small amounts, and I do not know whether it is lawful for me or not.' Abu Sufyan said: 'Whatever you have taken in the past and in what remains is lawful for you.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed and recognized her, and called her, and she came to him and sought refuge with him, and she said: 'Pardon what has passed, O Prophet of God; may God pardon you.' He said: 'nor commit adultery.' She said: 'Does a free woman commit adultery?' He said: 'nor kill their children.' Hind said: 'We raised them as children, and you killed them as adults, so you and they know best.' She meant that the Muslims had killed her son Hanzala ibn Abi Sufyan on the day of Badr. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) smiled. He said: 'nor bring forth a slander they have invented.' She said: 'By God, slander is a shameful matter, and you only command us to what is right and noble character.' He said: 'nor disobey you in what is right.' She said: 'By God, we did not sit in this gathering of ours with the intention of disobeying you in anything.'"

So His words ﴿nor disobey you in what is right﴾ comprehend everything that the Prophet (ﷺ) informs of and commands, of what returns to the obligations of Islam. In a hadith from Umm 'Atiyya: "Among that was: that we should not wail. She said: I said, 'O Messenger of God, except the family of so-and-so, for they helped me in the Jahiliyyah, so I must help them.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Except the family of so-and-so.'" This was a specific concession to Umm 'Atiyya and to those she named, and for a specific day.

His words ﴿then accept their pledge﴾ are the answer of the conditional (idhā) and a consequence of ﴿they pledge allegiance to you﴾, meaning: accept from them what they pledged to you about, because the pledge is from two sides for him, and for this reason it is formed in the mufā'ala pattern (the grammatical form of reciprocal action, as in bāya'a, "to pledge mutually").

﴿And ask God's forgiveness for them﴾ means: for what they fell short in during the Jahiliyyah of what was singled out for prohibition in the conditions of the pledge and other matters. For this reason the second object of the verb (istaghfir, "ask forgiveness") has been omitted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 60, verse 13:

Page 169
﴿O you who have believed, do not make allies of a people with whom Allah has been angry; they have despaired of the Hereafter, just as the disbelievers have despaired of the companions of the graves.﴾
After the surah had thoroughly set out the guidance for Muslims regarding what is obligatory in dealing with the polytheists, its conclusion gives guidance on how to deal with a people who are no less deserving of caution than the polytheists, namely the Jews. Thus the intended people are other than the polytheists, since their despair from the Hereafter is compared to the despair of the disbelievers, so it is determined that these are other than the polytheists, lest it be the comparison of a thing to itself.

Allah has described them as a people with whom Allah has been angry, and this is a description that is repeatedly applied to the Jews in the Qur'an, as in Surat al-Fatiha where they are described as those who earned anger. So this verse is like His saying, may He be exalted (﴿O you who have believed, do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as mockery and amusement from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 57]) in Surat al-'Uqud.

That is because the Jews of Khaybar were at that time neighbours of the Muslims of Medina. Al-Wahidi mentioned in Asbab al-Nuzul that it was revealed concerning some poor Muslims who worked for the Jews and kept company with them in order to obtain some of their fruits, and perhaps they informed the Jews of the affairs of the Muslims out of heedlessness and lack of caution, so Allah warned them not to make allies of them.

Al-yas (despair) is the non-expectation of a thing; when it is attached to a essence, it indicates the non-expectation of its existence. Since the Jews did not deny the Last Abode, the meaning of their despair from the Hereafter may be understood as turning away from working for the Hereafter, so that they are, in neglecting preparation for it, as those who despair of it. This is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted, concerning them: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter; so the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be aided﴾ [al-Baqara: 86] in Surat al-Baqara.

The comparison of their turning away with the despair of the disbelievers from the companions of the graves is based on the intensity of the turning away and the absence of reflection on the matter: their turning away from working for the benefit of the Hereafter is compared to the despair of the disbelievers from the life of the dead and the Resurrection, and in this there is a reprehension of the one compared. And ﴿from the companions of the graves﴾ on this view is connected to (yaisu) [they have despaired].  The disbelievers: the polytheists.

Page 170
It is also permissible that ﴿from the companions of the graves﴾ be an explanation of "the disbelievers", meaning the disbelievers who perished and saw that they had no share in the good of the Hereafter, so the turning away of the Jews from the Hereafter is compared to the despair of the disbelievers from the bliss of the Hereafter. The point of resemblance is the certainty of not benefiting from the Hereafter. The meaning is like the despair of the dead disbelievers, that is, despair from the Hereafter.
The thing compared to is known to the Muslims through belief, so the statement is a comparison of the perceptible to the intelligible.

In using "despair" for "turning away" there is also a kind of mushakala (correspondence of terms).

It is also possible that their despair from the Hereafter is used to mean their deprivation of the bliss of the Hereafter. The meaning then: We have made them despair of the Hereafter, in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and His meeting, those have despaired of My mercy﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 23] in Surat al-'Ankabut.

Among the earlier exegetes is one who took this verse to mean an emphasis of what is in the beginning of the surah, His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahana: 1]. So the people with whom Allah is angry are the polytheists, for they were described as enemies of Allah, and an enemy is one upon whom anger falls. This is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. And he took their despair from the Hereafter to be their denial of the Resurrection.

The comparison of their despair from the Hereafter with the despair of the disbelievers from the companions of the graves is that the despair of the living disbelievers is like the despair of the dead from among the disbelievers, that is, like the despair of their forebears who are in the graves, since during their lifetimes they were despairing of the Hereafter. Thus "min" is explanatory, describing the disbelievers, and is not connected to the verb (yaisa) [despaired]. There is therefore in the word "disbelievers" no display in place of the pronoun, for otherwise it would follow that a thing is compared with itself, as has been supposed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surat al-Saff

This surah is famous by the name "Surat al-Saff", and it was so called in the era of the Companions.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated with his chain to 'Abdullah ibn Salam: "Some people said: 'If we send someone to the Messenger of Allah to ask him about the most beloved of deeds'" ... until he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called those people together until he gathered them, and there was revealed concerning them (Surat Sabbaha lillahi, al-Saff)" — the hadith. Ibn Kathir narrated it, and by this it is titled in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, and likewise its name is written in the mushafs and in books of tafsir.

The reason for the name is the occurrence in it of the word "saffan" (in rows), which is the battle line, so the definite article is the definite of reference.

Al-Suyuti mentioned in al-Itqan that it is called "Surat al-Hawariyyin" (the Surah of the Disciples), but did not attribute it. Al-Alusi said it is called "Surat 'Isa" (the Surah of Jesus), but I have not found its attribution to a speaker. Its origin is with al-Tabarsi, so perhaps it was taken from a hadith he narrated on its virtue from Ubayy ibn Ka'b with the wording "Surat 'Isa". It is a hadith marked as fabricated (mawdu'), and al-Tabarsi frequently transmits fabricated hadiths. So its naming as "Surat al-Hawariyyin" is for the mention of the Disciples in it, and perhaps it is the first surah in which the word "al-Hawariyyin" was revealed.

If the name "Surat 'Isa" is established, it is because the name 'Isa is mentioned in it twice.

Page 172
It is Medinan according to the majority, as the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Salam supports. But from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata' it is reported that it is Meccan, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Fakhr followed this. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The most correct view is that it is Medinan, though it may be that something Meccan is in it."
Its occasion of revelation has been differed over, and whether it was revealed all at once or in successive parts.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi: "From 'Abdullah ibn Salam who said: A group of us, companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), sat and discussed, and we said: 'If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, we would do them.' So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Glorifies Allah whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise. O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 1-2]. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: The Messenger of Allah recited it to us." It was also narrated by al-Hakim, Ahmad in his Musnad, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Darimi, with the addition: "The Messenger of Allah recited it to us until he finished it," or "he recited it all."

This indicates that they were told, "Why do you say what you do not do?" before they failed to fulfil what they had promised, so the interrogative is used figuratively for warning against not fulfilling what they had vowed and promised.

From 'Ali ibn Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2], he said: Some of the believers, before jihad was enjoined, would say: "We wish that Allah, may He be exalted and majestic, would guide us to the most beloved of deeds to Him, so that we might do it." So Allah informed them that the most beloved of deeds is faith in Him and jihad against the people of His disobedience, who opposed faith and did not acknowledge it. When jihad was revealed, some of the believers disliked it and it weighed heavily upon them. So Allah, glorified and exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2].

Similar is from Abu Salih that the surah was revealed after they had been commanded to fight by verses other than those of this surah, and after they had promised to set out for jihad, then they held back from it and disliked it. This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the clearest and best suited to the structure of the verse. The interrogative in it is for rebuke and blame, and this fits His saying after it: ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3].

From Muqatil ibn Hayyan: The believers said: "If we knew the most beloved of deeds to Allah, we would act upon it." So Allah guided them, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row (saffan)﴾ [al-Saff: 4]. Then they were tested on the day of Uhud with that, and they turned their backs in flight. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]. Al-Wahidi attributed the like of this to the exegetes, and it implies that the beginning of the verse was revealed after its end.

From al-Kalbi: They said: "If we knew the most beloved of deeds to Allah, we would hasten to it." So there was revealed: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], the verse. Then they were tested on the day of Uhud, and there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2], reproaching them for not fulfilling. This implies that most of the surah came before the revelation of the verse which is at its beginning.

It is the 108th surah in the order of revelation according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Taghabun and before Surat al-Fath. Its revelation was after the battle of Uhud.

The number of its verses is fourteen, by agreement of the counters.
